It is often said that people with nothing to hide have nothing to fear from cameras. That reassurance rests on an assumption that is fast becoming (A) ____. A camera on a city street once registered only what passed in front of it; matching a face to a name required a human witness who fortuitously recognized it. Facial recognition software has removed that limit. Algorithms trained on millions of images can now compare a passing face against a database in a fraction of a second, and police forces in many countries deploy such systems to scour crowds, or footage amassed after a crime, for suspects.
Supporters cite arrests that might otherwise never have been made, whereas critics retort that the technology, for all its speed, is less trustworthy than its promotion implies. A 2019 study by a United States federal laboratory found that many algorithms generated erroneous matches far more often for some demographic groups than for others, and several Americans have been mistakenly arrested after a computer flagged them as suspects. Such errors, in other words, are (B) ____ rather than random.
Yet even a flawless system would raise a deeper problem — one that, I would argue, deserves more attention than any error rate. In a society where anyone can be identified anywhere, the anonymity in public that people have long taken for granted imperceptibly (C) ____. Legislators have responded unevenly: some American cities have barred their own agencies from deploying the technology, while the European Union's AI Act, adopted in 2024, stringently curtails real-time identification in public spaces by police, permitting it only in a narrow set of exceptional cases.

In 523 or 524, the Roman statesman Boethius, once the most influential official at the court of the Ostrogothic king Theodoric, was arrested on charges of treason and imprisoned near Pavia. While awaiting execution, he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy, a dialogue between himself and a majestic figure who materializes in his cell — Philosophy herself, in human form.
At first Boethius is (A) ____: he laments bitterly that he has lost his wealth, his honors, and his good name, and he cannot comprehend why a righteous man should suffer while the wicked prosper. Philosophy does not deny his misfortune, but she diagnoses his despair as a malady that calls for gentle remedies before strong ones. Fortune, she reminds him, spins a wheel; anyone who ascends it has no right to grumble when it carries him down again. The goods that Fortune bestows were never truly his, and their loss is therefore less (B) ____ than it appears. The true good, Philosophy contends, resides in what no one can confiscate: a mind ordered toward wisdom and virtue.
The book was transcribed and translated throughout the Middle Ages, and both King Alfred and Chaucer rendered it into English. Its enduring appeal may derive partly from its setting, for the claim that external fortune is (C) ____ carries far more weight when it comes from a man who has just lost everything.

In August 1653 the Dutch merchant ship Sperwer, bound for Japan, was wrecked in a tempest off the coast of Jeju Island. Of its crew of sixty-four, thirty-six reached the shore alive, among them Hendrick Hamel, the ship's bookkeeper — a man with no training as a writer and no reason to expect that his name would outlive the voyage. Joseon at the time admitted virtually no foreigners, and the survivors were forbidden to leave. They were taken to the capital, assigned to military units, and later scattered among provincial towns, where they dwelt for years as curiosities, sometimes begging to survive.
In 1666, after thirteen years in the country, Hamel and seven companions contrived to obtain a small boat and escaped to Nagasaki, where the Dutch kept an outpost. There Hamel compiled an account of the shipwreck and of the realm in which he had been detained, partly to support a claim for the wages owed to the crew for the years of their captivity. Published in the Netherlands in 1668, it became one of the first thorough descriptions of Korea accessible to European readers.
The account is invaluable precisely because its author was not a scholar: Hamel depicted what he encountered, from dwellings and punishments to the education of children and the way ordinary people treated strangers, without a theory to defend, and his sometimes mistaken judgments now tell historians as much about European assumptions as about Korea itself.

(A) In December 1817, the young poet John Keats wrote a letter to his brothers describing an attribute he believed every eminent writer possessed. He called it negative capability: the capacity for being in uncertainties, mysteries, and doubts without any irritable reaching after fact and reason.
(B) Keats found the supreme example in Shakespeare, whose plays give voice to murderers and saints, fools and kings, without ever settling into a single verdict on them. A mediocre writer, Keats implied, cannot endure leaving a question open and hastens to resolve it, sacrificing the richness of experience for the solace of an answer.
(C) Keats had trained as a surgeon's apprentice and qualified as an apothecary before abandoning medicine for poetry, a decision that dismayed the guardian who controlled the family's finances.
(D) The phrase has since migrated far beyond poetry. Psychoanalysts have adopted it to denote the patience a therapist needs to sit with a patient's confusion rather than imposing an early interpretation, and instructors in design invoke it to admonish students against settling on the first workable solution.
(E) What these uses share is a suspicion of premature certainty. Negative capability is not a refusal to think but a discipline of thinking — the willingness to let a difficulty remain difficult long enough to be understood.

Last spring, a dozen parents in my daughter's class met in a school gym and signed a short pledge: none of us would give our children a smartphone before the age of fourteen. It was not an act of nostalgia, since most of us work on screens all day and rely on them more than we care to concede. What united us was a more basic fear — that whichever family held out alone would be turning its child into an outcast.
That fear is the engine of the whole problem, for few parents I know genuinely want their eleven-year-olds carrying a device that offers endless video and the ceaseless judgment of classmates. They give in because everyone else seems to be giving in, and a pact, by binding families to one another, breaks that spiral, which is why comparable agreements have proliferated among parents in Britain and elsewhere since 2024, when the social psychologist Jonathan Haidt's book The Anxious Generation drew considerable attention to escalating anxiety among adolescents.
I do not contend that the evidence is conclusive; researchers still dispute how much of that surge can be attributed to smartphones. Nor is our pledge a ban on technology, since our children can still text from a rudimentary phone and use the family computer. But I would rather we err on the side of a prolonged childhood than discover, belatedly, that the skeptics were mistaken. Waiting, after all, can be undone. A lost childhood cannot.

Few paintings so thoroughly defeat the (A) ____ glance as Hans Holbein's The Ambassadors, painted in 1533 and now in the National Gallery in London. Visitors who stand directly in front of it behold two sumptuously attired young Frenchmen posed beside a set of shelves cluttered with objects that proclaim learning and affluence: a celestial globe, a terrestrial globe, sundials, a book of arithmetic, a hymnbook, and a lute. Across the floor at the men's feet, however, stretches an eerie pale shape that looks at first like a smear or a bone. Only when the viewer walks to the side of the painting and looks back at an oblique angle does the shape (B) ____ into a human skull.
The technique, called anamorphosis, deliberately distorts an image so that it can be seen correctly only from one viewpoint. Holbein used it to convey a message that the remainder of the picture seems contrived to conceal: the instruments and books celebrate human knowledge, but the skull reminds the viewer that death awaits every scholar and statesman, however accomplished, and even the lute, on close inspection, has a snapped string — a conventional emblem of discord.
Some historians speculate that the painting was meant to hang beside a doorway or staircase, so that people leaving the room would glimpse the skull as they passed. If so, the effect was carefully (C) ____: the viewer, having admired the splendor of worldly achievement face to face, would discover its limits only on turning away.

What would you do with something the whole world could not afford to lose? Before I talk about my own work, I want to tell you about a building most of you will never visit. It is carved into a mountain on Spitsbergen, an island in the Norwegian Arctic about thirteen hundred kilometers from the North Pole, and since it opened in 2008 the Svalbard Global Seed Vault has received duplicate samples of crop seeds from gene banks around the world — well over a million of them by now — and safeguarded them in chambers kept at about minus eighteen degrees Celsius.
People sometimes dub it the doomsday vault, as if it were waiting for the end of the world. The truth is less sensational and more pragmatic: in 2015, researchers whose gene bank near Aleppo had been disrupted by the Syrian civil war asked for some of their deposited seeds back; they used them to rebuild their collections in Lebanon and Morocco, and later returned fresh samples to the mountain. The vault, in other words, worked exactly as intended: not as a monument to catastrophe but as an ordinary backup copy.
I tell you this story because many of you are about to embark on careers in agriculture and science, and you will be tempted to think that consequential work must be glamorous. Most of it is not. It is painstaking, repetitive, and easy to overlook, like labeling a box of seeds and placing it on a cold shelf in case someone, someday, needs it.

More than two thousand years ago, the Chinese philosopher Zhuangzi chronicled a dream. He dreamed that he was a butterfly — flitting blithely from flower to flower, wholly oblivious that he was Zhuangzi. Then he awoke and found himself, corporeal and unmistakable, lying in bed. But now he could not ascertain whether he was Zhuangzi who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming that it was Zhuangzi.
Western readers often construe the story as a precursor of a skeptical conundrum: how can I prove that I am not dreaming at this very moment? Descartes, nearly two thousand years later, would formulate an analogous question, yet Zhuangzi does not appear perturbed: he offers no argument to escape the doubt and evinces no inclination to find one. He simply avers that between Zhuangzi and the butterfly there must be some distinction, and calls the passage from one to the other <u>the transformation of things</u>.
For Zhuangzi, the insight lies less in what we can know than in how we cling to who we are. If the self can flow from one form into another, then clinging tenaciously to any single form, whether as a scholar, an official, or even a living body, may be a source of unnecessary suffering rather than of security.

For much of the past decade, the subscription appeared to be the consummate business model. Instead of selling a product once, companies could charge a modest fee every month for software, films, music, meal kits, and even car features such as heated seats. Investors relished the predictable revenue, and consumers savored the convenience of never having to contemplate renewing anything.
That very convenience has begun to curdle. Surveys in several countries suggest that many households underestimate how much they spend on subscriptions, often paying for services they rarely use. Some companies have made signing up a matter of one click while concealing the cancellation option behind phone calls, bewildering menus, and eleventh-hour discount offers, designs for which regulators have a name — dark patterns. In 2024 the Federal Trade Commission in Washington promulgated a regulation obliging businesses to make cancelling as easy as signing up, a rule that business groups challenged and that a federal appeals court struck down in July 2025.
Consumers, meanwhile, have begun to adapt on their own. Streaming services report that a burgeoning share of customers sign up for a single month to watch one series, cancel, and return later for the next. Services have responded with cheaper plans that carry advertisements, reviving the very commercials that many people had subscribed in order to avoid. The subscription, it appears, is entering a more ____ phase, in which customers treat each monthly payment not as a habit but as a decision.

In Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon, a samurai is discovered slain in a forest, and four witnesses give their accounts of what happened — a bandit, the samurai's wife, a woodcutter, and the dead man himself, speaking through a medium. The accounts Ⓐ<u>conflict</u> on almost every important point; several of the speakers depict events in ways that flatter their own conduct, and the film never discloses which version is true.
The film was an improbable success, garnering the top prize at the Venice Film Festival in 1951 and introducing many Western audiences to Japanese cinema. Its title has since permeated the vocabulary of law, journalism, and social science. The Rashomon effect denotes the way disparate observers of the same event can produce Ⓑ<u>contradictory</u> yet sincere accounts of it.
The phrase is often misused, however. It does not mean that there is no truth, or that every account is equally Ⓒ<u>valid</u>. Something did transpire in the forest. What the film Ⓓ<u>dramatizes</u> is how memory and self-interest shape testimony. Courts and historians who contend with conflicting witnesses do not simply abandon the search for facts; instead, they collate accounts, scrutinize physical evidence, and weigh each witness's motives. Kurosawa's achievement was to make that difficulty Ⓔ<u>trivial</u> for audiences, so that viewers leave the theater feeling the uncertainty rather than merely understanding it.

Blaise Pascal, the seventeenth-century French mathematician who helped found the theory of probability, left among his unfinished notes an argument that has provoked readers ever since. It concerns belief in God, but its form is that of a bet.
Reason, Pascal granted, cannot settle whether God exists. Yet we cannot simply decline to choose, since living as though there were no God is itself a choice. We must therefore weigh the possible outcomes. If we believe and God exists, we gain an infinite reward; if we believe and God does not exist, we forfeit little — perhaps a few worldly pleasures; if we refuse to believe and God exists, the loss is infinite. Since even a negligible probability of an infinite gain outweighs any finite cost, Pascal inferred, a rational gambler should bet on God. The argument does not claim to prove that God exists; it claims to show that belief is the ____ choice.
Critics have lodged manifold objections: some query which God one should bet on, since many religions promise rewards and punishments, while others doubt that belief can be adopted at will merely because it is advantageous. Pascal anticipated this last objection: a person who cannot believe, he ventured, should commence by acting as believers do, in the hope that conviction would follow.
Whatever its merits as theology, the wager has had a long career in other domains. Decision theorists cite it as an early exemplar of reasoning about expected value, and some writers on environmental policy have co-opted its structure to contend that the cost of acting on an uncertain threat may be trivial compared with the cost of disregarding it.

Not long ago, a programmer who answered emails from a beach in Bali was doing something of dubious legality. Most tourist visas prohibit holders from working, and few governments had made provision for people who earned salaries from employers in one country while living in another, until the pandemic, which rendered remote work commonplace for millions of office workers, changed that.
Estonia was among the first countries to offer a visa tailored to such workers, inaugurating one in 2020. A multitude of others have followed — from Caribbean islands to European states such as Portugal and Spain; in Asia, Japan and South Korea both introduced their own versions in 2024. The customary arrangement entitles a foreigner to reside for a year or more, provided that he or she can demonstrate a steady income from abroad above a set threshold. Governments hope that these visitors will spend their foreign salaries locally without depriving residents of jobs.
The repercussions have been mixed: cafés and landlords in coveted destinations have welcomed the newcomers, but residents of some cities, notably Lisbon and Mexico City, lament that affluent remote workers have helped drive rents beyond what local wages can sustain. Tax authorities confront dilemmas of their own, since it is often unclear which country is entitled to tax income earned by someone who lives in one place, works for a company in another, and holds citizenship in a third.
These tensions raise a question that many governments are only beginning to grapple with: whether the rules they adopted so eagerly now need to be rewritten.

In the 1490s, a scholar named Aldus Manutius set up a printing house in Venice with an unconventional ambition: to put the great works of ancient Greek literature into print before the manuscripts that preserved them were lost. He engaged Greek scholars, many of them exiles, as editors, and over the following two decades his press issued the first printed editions of Aristotle, Plato, Sophocles, and many others.
His most enduring contributions, however, pertained to the form of the book rather than its content. In 1501 he published an edition of the Roman poet Virgil in a format small enough to carry in a saddlebag or a large pocket. Books of the period were customarily ponderous volumes meant to rest on a desk or a lectern; Aldus's (A) ____ editions made it feasible for cultivated readers to take literature with them on journeys and into gardens. To accommodate more words on these diminutive pages, he had his type cutter, Francesco Griffo, design a slanted, compact typeface modeled on refined handwriting, the precursor of what we now call italic type.
Aldus also helped establish the modern semicolon, which appeared in a book he printed in 1496, and he favored a cleaner, more (B) ____ style of punctuation than the cluttered marks of many manuscripts. Readers rarely notice such conventions — they simply expect them — and that we take them for granted is perhaps the best measure of how thoroughly the Aldine press reshaped the experience of reading.

In August 2024, a federal judge in Washington ruled that Google had illegally maintained a monopoly in online search. The case, brought by the United States Department of Justice together with a group of states, was the most consequential antitrust trial against a technology company in more than two decades. Pivotal to the ruling were the billions of dollars Google paid each year to companies such as Apple and to makers of web browsers so that its search engine would be the default on their devices. Those payments, the judge found, had excluded rivals from the most crucial channels by which users access a search engine.
Google argued that people use its search engine because it is the best — not because they are compelled to — and that switching to a rival takes only a few taps. The court was not persuaded that defaults are so easily overridden. Most users, it noted, never alter the settings that come with their phones, which is precisely why companies are eager to pay so lavishly to control them.
The case reflects a broader shift. For decades, antitrust enforcement in the United States focused chiefly on whether a company's conduct inflated prices for consumers. Since search engines are free to use, that criterion made it difficult to demonstrate any harm. The newer doctrine holds that harm can manifest in other forms, such as reduced innovation or diminished choice, and that a firm can impair competition even while its product costs users nothing.

In 1872, a young assistant at the British Museum named George Smith was sifting through clay tablets that had been shipped to London from the ruins of Nineveh, the ancient Assyrian capital. Smith had left school at fourteen to apprentice as a banknote engraver, but he had taught himself to read cuneiform during lunch breaks spent in the museum's galleries, and his proficiency had earned him a post there.
One fragmentary tablet recounted the story of a man who, warned by a god, built a colossal boat, loaded it with his family and animals, and survived a flood that annihilated the rest of humanity, after which he sent out birds to find dry land. Smith discerned at once how closely the story resembled the account of Noah in the Book of Genesis. When he unveiled his findings in London in December of that year, the prime minister, William Gladstone, was in the audience.
The discovery caused a sensation. A newspaper, The Daily Telegraph, financed a journey for Smith to the site of Nineveh to search for the missing pieces, and remarkably he found a fragment that filled part of the gap within about a week of starting to dig. The tablet proved to belong to a far lengthier poem — the work now known as the Epic of Gilgamesh. Smith himself did not live to see the epic widely acclaimed; he succumbed to illness in 1876 during his third expedition, still in his thirties.

In 1325, a twenty-one-year-old legal scholar named Ibn Battuta left his home in Tangier to make the pilgrimage to Mecca. He anticipated an absence of perhaps a year and a half, yet he did not return, as it turned out, for nearly a quarter of a century. Following a <u>wayward</u> itinerary that took him across North Africa, through the Middle East, down the coast of East Africa, across Central Asia to India, and possibly as far as China, he traversed, by some reckonings, more than one hundred thousand kilometers — far more than Marco Polo.
His travels were facilitated by the immense network of Muslim societies that sprawled across much of the known world. As a trained judge, he could procure employment and hospitality almost anywhere Islamic law prevailed; in Delhi the sultan appointed him a judge, and he later held the same post in the Maldives.
After he at last resettled in Morocco, its sovereign commissioned him to record his journeys, whereupon Ibn Battuta dictated his memories to a court scholar, Ibn Juzayy, who wrought them into a book conventionally known as the Rihla, or Travels. Because the account was composed from memory years after the events, historians regard some of its details with circumspection, and a few passages appear to have been borrowed from earlier writers; its panorama of the fourteenth-century world, however, is unrivaled.

Japan has a housing problem that many countries would envy — too many homes. A government survey released in 2024 counted about nine million vacant houses, known as akiya, a record that constitutes nearly one in seven dwellings in the country. The figure Ⓐ<u>reflects</u> a dwindling and aging population, as well as a long-standing preference for new construction over old houses, which in Japan often lose most of their value within a few decades.
Empty houses are not merely a waste. Left unattended, they decay, become infested with pests, and can Ⓑ<u>collapse</u> in earthquakes or typhoons, endangering their neighbors. Because owners have long paid lower property taxes on land with a house standing on it than on vacant land, many have had little incentive to Ⓒ<u>preserve</u> derelict buildings, even when they have no intention of ever inhabiting them. Inheritance aggravates matters: houses pass to heirs who reside in distant cities and remain undecided about what to do with them.
Local governments have responded in diverse ways: some run online listings, known as akiya banks, that offer vacant houses for sale, sometimes for almost nothing, and furnish subsidies to young families inclined to relocate to the countryside and Ⓓ<u>renovate</u> them. Foreign buyers, drawn by stories of homes sold for the price of a used car, have added to the interest. Yet many akiya stand in remote villages with few jobs and waning services, and a house acquired for a pittance cannot by itself Ⓔ<u>reverse</u> the decline of the community around it.

On 13 January 1898, the Paris newspaper L'Aurore devoted its front page to an open letter from the novelist Emile Zola to the President of France. Its headline — J'accuse — became one of the most renowned in the history of journalism. Zola <u>excoriated</u> the army officers and officials who had condemned Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish captain convicted of passing military secrets to Germany, and who had then shielded the officer whom the evidence implicated as the real culprit.
Zola knew full well what he was jeopardizing, since by naming individuals and accusing them of deliberate injustice, he invited a prosecution for libel, and he was in fact convicted and fled to England to avoid prison. Yet the letter accomplished its objective, turning a closed military case into a national debate that polarized France for years, pitting those who placed the honor of the army above the rights of one man against those who insisted that justice could not be sacrificed to institutional pride. Dreyfus was exonerated in 1906.
The affair is often said to have given birth to the modern figure of the intellectual: a writer or scholar who draws on a reputation acquired in one domain to intervene in political questions. Whether that role is admirable or presumptuous has been disputed ever since.

For decades, the map of international education had a familiar shape: students from Asia, Africa, and Latin America gravitated toward four English-speaking destinations — the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia — which together hosted a large share of the world's internationally mobile students. Universities in those countries came to depend on the fees these students paid, which were often far higher than those charged to domestic students.
That map, however, is now being redrawn, for since 2024 Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia have all moved to restrict numbers. Canada announced a cap on new study permits early that year, citing the strain on housing. The United Kingdom stopped most taught master's students from bringing family members with them, and Australia raised its student visa fee and sought to limit enrollments. Governments portrayed these measures as responses to housing shortages and public anxiety about migration, but universities warned that lost fees would compel them to curtail courses and staff.
Meanwhile, other destinations have stepped forward: several countries in continental Europe now offer degree programs taught entirely in English, often at little or no tuition cost. In Asia, governments have set ambitious targets; South Korea, for instance, has proclaimed the objective of attracting three hundred thousand international students by 2027. For students, the result is a more expansive array of choices; for the traditional destinations, it is a competition that they, having dominated the field for so long, once assumed they could not lose.

In 416 BCE, during the long war between Athens and Sparta, an Athenian fleet arrived at the small island of Melos, which had tried to remain neutral, and before launching an assault, the Athenian envoys conferred with the island's magistrates. The historian Thucydides, who reconstructed the exchange, presents it as a debate between two conceptions of how states ought to comport themselves.
The Melians appealed to justice: they had done Athens no wrong, and the gods, they hoped, would favor the side that was in the right. The Athenians, however, refused to argue on those terms, declaring that questions of justice arise only between equals in power; otherwise <u>the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must</u>. Submission, they added, would spare Melos from destruction, while resistance would gain it nothing.
The Melians, unwilling to buy their safety at such a price, refused to surrender; after a siege the city fell, and the Athenians killed the men and enslaved the women and children. Thucydides offers no comment, but he places the episode just before his account of the Athenian expedition to Sicily, the overreaching campaign that ended in catastrophe and helped bring about the city's eventual defeat. Many readers have taken the arrangement as a tacit verdict — a power that recognizes no limit but its own strength may in the end be undone by it.

In 1605 Miguel de Cervantes published the first part of Don Quixote, the story of an aging gentleman who devours so many tales of chivalry that he sets out to become a knight himself. The book was an immediate success, and readers awaited its continuation avidly; before Cervantes could complete it, however, a rival forestalled him. In 1614 a sequel appeared under the name Alonso Fernandez de Avellaneda, a pseudonym whose owner has never been identified with certainty. Its preface mocked Cervantes for his age and — more cruelly — for the hand he had lost the use of in battle.
Cervantes took his revenge inside the fiction itself: in his own second part, published in 1615, the characters learn that a false history of their adventures is circulating. Don Quixote, leafing through a copy, finds it rife with errors, and because the impostor's Quixote had traveled to the jousts at Zaragoza, the real one changes his plans and goes to Barcelona instead, determined to expose the other book as a fabrication. Later he even meets a character from the rival novel and persuades him to make a formal declaration that the Quixote and Sancho he had known were frauds.
In this episode Cervantes does something remarkably modern, for rather than simply <u>upbraiding</u> the forger in a preface, he folds the dispute into the story, letting his characters become cognizant that they have a public life in print. The theft, in a sense, provoked one of the earliest and most whimsical experiments in fiction that reflects on its own making.

On 19 July 2024, millions of computers around the world abruptly crashed and displayed the blue error screen that Windows users dread. Airlines Ⓐ<u>grounded</u> flights, hospitals postponed operations, and banks and broadcasters strove to keep running. The cause was not a cyberattack but a faulty software update from CrowdStrike — a cybersecurity company whose program runs deep inside the Windows operating system on many corporate machines. Microsoft later estimated that about 8.5 million devices had been Ⓑ<u>affected</u>.
The update itself was small, and the company withdrew it within about an hour and a half. Repairing the damage took far longer. Because the affected machines could not start normally, technicians often had to fix them one by one, sometimes in person, and some organizations needed days to recover fully.
The episode exposed a Ⓒ<u>paradox</u> of modern computing: security software is given deep access to a system precisely so that it can protect it, but that same access means a single error can propagate with alarming velocity. And because a few firms supply such software to a large share of the world's businesses, the global economy has become Ⓓ<u>resilient</u> to the mistakes of a handful of companies. Some specialists now urge organizations to test updates on a few machines before installing them everywhere and to keep backup systems that do not share the same Ⓔ<u>weaknesses</u>.

Ask a reader to name a tale from The Thousand and One Nights, and the answer is likely to be Aladdin or Ali Baba. It is one of the ironies of literary history that neither story appears in any of the surviving medieval Arabic manuscripts of the collection.
The Nights reached Europe through the French scholar Antoine Galland, whose translation began to appear in 1704 and became a sensation almost overnight. Galland's main source was a Syrian manuscript copied centuries earlier, but it broke off long before the promised thousand and one nights were complete, and readers and publishers demanded more. In 1709 Galland met Hanna Diyab, a young Maronite Christian from Aleppo who was visiting Paris and who told him a number of stories from memory, which Galland noted down in his diary. Several, including the tales we now know as Aladdin and Ali Baba, appeared in later volumes of the translation, retold in Galland's elegant French.
For nearly three centuries, Diyab's part was almost forgotten, while scholars searched in vain for the Arabic originals of these orphan tales, and some manuscripts that purported to contain them turned out to be translations back into Arabic from Galland's French. Only in recent decades, through the study of the travel memoir Diyab himself wrote, has the young storyteller begun to garner credit.
The history of the Nights is thus a history of collaboration across languages — one in which the line between translating and creating is difficult to delineate. The most famous Arabian tales in the world may owe their shape as much to a Syrian traveler and a French scholar as to any medieval source.
